articles.title: Put a human checkpoint on the agent actions you cannot undo
articles.excerpt: Your agent can solve a captcha faster than a person can. ETH Zurich researchers proved the point in 2024 when a fine-tuned YOLOv8 passed 100% of reCAPTCHAv2 challenges, and the industry responded by m…
articles.body: Your agent can solve a captcha faster than a person can. ETH Zurich researchers proved the point in 2024 when a fine-tuned YOLOv8 passed 100% of reCAPTCHAv2 challenges, and the industry responded by moving to invisible behavioral checks and signed agent identity (Web Bot Auth, RFC 9421). The "prove you are human" puzzle is dead as a business and dying as a technique. What is not dead is the decision you cannot take back. Refunds, wires, deletions, deploys, legal replies. When an agent is about to do one of those, the right move is not a better prompt. It is a pause, a human decision, and a record. This post builds that checkpoint from scratch: a risk policy, a pause primitive, signed approval links, a timeout default, and an audit log. About 120 lines of Python, no external services.
articles.author: Tej Pandya

articles.title: URL Encoding: 6 Mistakes That Break Your Query Strings
articles.excerpt: Broken links and missing query parameters are often an encoding problem. These are the mistakes worth knowing. encodeURI leaves ? & = # alone, so it is for whole URLs. encodeURIComponent encodes them,…
articles.body: Broken links and missing query parameters are often an encoding problem. These are the mistakes worth knowing. 1. encodeURI vs encodeURIComponent encodeURI leaves ? & = # alone, so it is for whole URLs. encodeURIComponent encodes them, so it is for individual values. Using the wrong one either breaks the URL or the value. 2. Double encoding Encoding an already encoded value turns %20 into %2520 . Encode once, at the last step before sending. 3. Plus vs %20 In form data + means space, but in a URL path it is a literal plus. Mixing them silently changes your data. 4. Unicode and emoji Non-ASCII characters are encoded as UTF-8 bytes, so one emoji becomes up to 12 characters. Check length limits after encoding. 5.

articles.title: Your AppArmor Profile Is Doing Nothing: Practical Path Confinement on Linux
articles.excerpt: Your AppArmor Profile Is Doing Nothing: Practical Path Confinement on Linux On the Debian 13 host I used for this article, aa-status reports 106 loaded profiles, 7 in enforce mode, and 23 in complain…
articles.body: Your AppArmor Profile Is Doing Nothing: Practical Path Confinement on Linux On the Debian 13 host I used for this article, aa-status reports 106 loaded profiles, 7 in enforce mode, and 23 in complain mode. The kernel module is enabled, the service manager is happy, and the shell I ran the checks from still reports unconfined . That gap is not a bug in AppArmor. It is the normal consequence of a mental model mismatch. AppArmor is not a label on an inode, and a profile is not "security" in the abstract. It is a list of path permissions attached to a specific executable, enforced from the moment that executable is called. If any link in that chain is wrong, you get a loaded profile that confines nothing.

articles.body: When someone pastes one of my launch pages into Slack, WhatsApp or X, the preview card is the first thing anyone sees of it. For a launch site that's kind of the whole point. The founder shares their listing, the card shows up, people click. I've checked a lot of things on my own pages over the last few weeks: status codes, sitemaps, canonicals, cache headers on the HTML. I had never checked what a preview bot actually gets when it asks for the image. So this morning I did. 13 of my sites, 130 pages (the homepage plus 9 pages spread across each sitemap). For every page I fetched the HTML with a facebookexternalhit/1.1 user agent, read the og: and twitter: tags, then downloaded the first og:image and opened it with Pillow to get its real size.

articles.title: On this day in space! Nov. 24, 1947: The US Navy launches the 1st Aerobee sounding rocket, but it didn't reach space
articles.excerpt: On Nov. 24, 1947, the U.S. Navy launched the first Aerobee rocket into the sky, but it never reached space. Here's why it mattered.
articles.body: On Nov. 24, 1947, the U.S. Navy launched the first Aerobee rocket into the sky, but it never reached space. Aerobee was a suborbital sounding rocket designed to study Earth's atmosphere . After World War 2, the United States started reusing erman V-2 rockets for this kind of research. When they started running out of V-2 rockets , the United States constructed its own rockets that were similar but cheaper to build and to launch. In the weeks leading up to the first Aerobee mission, three test flights were launched. Those tests used a dummy version of Aerobee with a live booster to see if the two stages would separate properly. On Aerobee's first real flight, the rocket flew about 35 miles high. That's below the 62-mile (100 kilometers) upper limit for the boundary of space .

articles.title: 'Blade Runner 2099' executive producers talk architectural easter eggs and franchise continuity for Prime Video's new sci-fi series (interview)
articles.excerpt: 'Today, sitting here in November of 2026, the world is catching up quicker to the world of 'Blade Runner.''
articles.body: Prime Video's new " Blade Runner 2099 " series arrives Nov. 25, 2026, and it flips the cyberpunk universe on its head. The new show casts replicants as the dominant species on Earth, with humans relegated to second-class citizens after a global uprising. This dreary dystopian cyberpunk realm originates from sci-fi legend Phillip K. Dick's 1968 novel, "Do Androids Dream of Electric Sheep?," and was then so vividly brought to life in Ridley Scott’s seminal 1982 adaptation, " Blade Runner ." The 2017 sequel, "Blade Runner 2049," was directed by "Arrival’s" and "Dune’s" Denis Villeneuve.
